flashcards.q: Define G, M, and P in Go's scheduler, and state what actually bounds parallel Go-code execution.
flashcards.a: G=goroutine (lightweight user-space work unit), M=OS thread (kernel-scheduled), P=logical processor context (exactly GOMAXPROCS of them, each with a local run queue). An M must hold a P to run Go code, so P count -- not M count -- bounds true parallelism.

flashcards.q: Can the number of live OS threads (Ms) exceed GOMAXPROCS?
flashcards.a: Yes -- when a goroutine makes a blocking syscall, its M's P is detached and handed to another M so other goroutines keep running, so live M count can temporarily exceed GOMAXPROCS under blocking-syscall load.

flashcards.q: Describe Go's goroutine stack growth mechanism and why it requires precise compiler support.
flashcards.a: Starts at 2KB; a function-entry check detects insufficient room and triggers allocating a bigger stack, copying old contents over, and rewriting every pointer that referenced the old stack's addresses to point into the new one. Only safe because compiler-generated stack maps tell the runtime precisely which stack words are pointers -- unavailable to a naive C runtime.

flashcards.q: What changed in Go 1.14's scheduler and what bug class did it fix?
flashcards.a: Introduced asynchronous preemption via OS signals, interrupting a goroutine at arbitrary points instead of only at function-call safe points -- fixed tight loops with no calls starving peer goroutines on the same P indefinitely (a real pre-1.14 bug class).

flashcards.q: What was the container-aware GOMAXPROCS problem fixed in Go 1.25?
flashcards.a: Pre-1.25, GOMAXPROCS defaulted to the HOST's total core count even inside a CPU-limited container/cgroup, causing scheduler oversubscription and cgroup CFS throttling-induced tail latency. Go 1.25 made the default container-aware.

flashcards.q: What is a V8 hidden class (Map) and why does property-addition ORDER matter, not just the final property set?
flashcards.a: A hidden class encodes an object's property set and storage offsets, shared by objects built via the same addition sequence. Two objects with identical final properties but different addition orders can end up with DIFFERENT hidden classes, defeating fast fixed-offset access -- consistent construction order (e.g. via a shared constructor) is what actually matters.

flashcards.q: Distinguish monomorphic, polymorphic, and megamorphic inline cache states.
flashcards.a: Monomorphic: one hidden class ever seen, fastest fixed-offset access. Polymorphic: a small bounded number of shapes (commonly up to ~4), still fast via a small dispatch table. Megamorphic: too many shapes, fast path abandoned entirely, generic slow lookup, and TurboFan won't type-specialize that site.

flashcards.q: What are Ignition and TurboFan in V8?
flashcards.a: Ignition: bytecode interpreter that runs all JS initially and records type feedback per call/access site into a per-function FeedbackVector. TurboFan: the optimizing JIT that compiles hot functions using that feedback into speculative, type-specialized machine code.

flashcards.q: What happens when a TurboFan-optimized function's speculative shape/type assumption breaks at runtime?
flashcards.a: V8 deoptimizes: discards the optimized machine code, reconstructs an equivalent interpreter-level stack frame, and resumes execution in Ignition -- architecturally the same pattern as JVM C2 deoptimization and CPython's adaptive-interpreter de-specialization.

flashcards.q: Why is spawning 100,000 goroutines routine in Go but spawning 100,000 OS threads is not?
flashcards.a: Memory: 100,000 goroutines at 2KB starting stack each is roughly 200MB; 100,000 OS threads at a typical 1-8MB default stack each is roughly 200GB-800GB. Goroutine stacks also start tiny and grow on demand rather than reserving a large fixed size upfront.

flashcards.q: How do you diagnose a V8/Node.js function that suddenly got slower with no code change?
flashcards.a: Suspect a shift to megamorphic inline caches or a deoptimization triggered by a change in the data flowing through the function (new object shapes, type changes). Diagnose with --trace-deopt (deopt events/reasons) and --trace-ic (IC state transitions) rather than guessing.

flashcards.q: What is Go's work-stealing scheduling behavior, and what happens when it fails?
flashcards.a: An idle P steals roughly half of another P's local run queue rather than sitting idle, keeping all GOMAXPROCS logical processors busy under uneven load. A global run queue exists only as a fallback/overflow, not the common scheduling path.

flashcards.q: What does a Go write barrier do during concurrent GC marking, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Extra work on every pointer write during the concurrent mark phase to catch the mutator concurrently mutating the object graph in a way that could hide a live object from the collector (a tricolor-invariant violation) â€” the real, always-on cost of running marking concurrently with the mutator instead of stopping the world for it.

flashcards.q: Name V8's compilation tiers between Ignition and TurboFan, and why they exist.
flashcards.a: Sparkplug (fast baseline JIT, compiles Ignition bytecode to unoptimized machine code almost immediately) and Maglev (mid-tier optimizing compiler). They exist for the same reason the JVM's C1 exists between its interpreter and C2: TurboFan's compile cost is too slow to apply to every warm function, pure interpretation too slow for functions that run enough to matter.

flashcards.q: In Node.js, does a resolved Promise's .then() callback or an earlier-scheduled setTimeout(fn, 0) run first?
flashcards.a: The Promise callback always runs first â€” V8's microtask queue is fully drained after every callback the event loop runs, before it proceeds to the next macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, setImmediate), regardless of scheduling order. A recursively self-scheduling microtask chain can starve timers/I/O entirely.
